study.title: Ezekiel 5 - Judgement measured on Jerusalem
study.overview: Ezekiel 5 presents a prophetic dramatization of God's judgment against Jerusalem. The prophet, using a symbolic act with shaved hair, shows that the city will be hit by famine, sword and dispersion. Then the Lord Himself interprets the sign: Jerusalem, despite having received a privileged position among the nations, rebelled more than the peoples around, profaned the sanctuary and rejected the divine statutes. The chapter insists that judgment is not arbitrary; it responds to the broken covenant and culminates in public shame before the nations.

outline.title: The sign of shaved and distributed hair
outline.explanation: God sends Ezekiel to shave hair and beard with a sharp sword, weigh the strands and divide them into three parts, with a small portion preserved in the clothes. The gesture announces proportional and diversified destruction: part dies in the siege, part by the sword and part is scattered in the wind, although there remains a small remnant, still exposed to suffering.

outline.title: Jerusalem accused and sentenced
outline.explanation: The Lord declares that Jerusalem was placed among the nations, but he rebelled more than them against the divine judgments and statutes. Therefore, God Himself stands against the city and promises visible judgments, without relief, including extreme hunger, cannibalism, plague, sword and dispersion. The stated purpose is to reveal that the judgment came from the Lord and that his wrath was fully executed.

outline.title: Public dishonor among the nations
outline.explanation: The city will become ruin, humiliation, and an object of astonishment for the peoples around. The infamy of Jerusalem will serve as a lesson and warning, because the judgments of God will be seen as acts of wrath and wrath, confirming the seriousness of the divine word.

outline.title: The last blows: famine, beasts, pestilence and sword
outline.explanation: The chapter ends by extending the picture of devastation with starvation images such as deadly arrows, shortages of bread, ferocious animals, sterility, plague, blood and sword. The closure reaffirms the absolute authority of the sentence: 'I, the Lord, have spoken.'

study.context: The text interprets Jerusalem in a key to alliance. The notes highlight that the Lord accuses his people with proper language of the covenant made in Sinai and renewed in Deuteronomy. Debedience is not only presented as a generic moral failure, but as a rejection of God's decrees and statutes, especially in worship, with the desecration of the temple. Thus, the chapter works as an announcement that the curses of disobedience now come into force.
study.theology: The theology of the chapter highlights, first, the holiness of God and his justice: judgment is measured, intentionally and morally grounded. Second, the responsibility of the covenant is evidenced: spiritual privileges increase guilt when there is rebellion. Third, the text shows that God disciplines in a historical and concrete way, using hunger, sword, dispersion and public shame. Fourth, the remnant preserved in small portion points out that judgment does not totally eliminate God's purpose for his people, although preservation here is accompanied by suffering. Finally, the chapter teaches that idolatry and the profanity of worship bring serious consequences, because they reach the center of the relationship between God and his people.

scholarViews.insight: The act of shaving and distributing the hair shows God's measured judgment in three forms: hunger, violent death and exile.
Jerusalem is explained as the sign itself; the city will be stripped and naked as a shaved head, portraying its total humiliation.
Hair represents the people, and the rite points to the calamities, shame and dispersion that would come upon the nation.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the seriousness of disobedience when it occurs within the community that has received greater light and privilege?
How does the profanation of worship appear here as central sin, and not just as secondary detail?
How can we recognize today signs of God's discipline without falling into hasty or simplistic conclusions?
study.practice: This chapter calls for a sincere assessment of fidelity to God in worship, obedience and public life. The concrete application is to abandon spiritual presumption, confess persistent sins and treat seriously all that profanes worship and distorts the covenant with the Lord. It also recalls that divine discipline must produce reverent fear and repentance, not indifference. For the community of faith, the practical answer is to examine whether obedience is only external or whether it really honors the statutes of God.
study.uncertainty: The chapter uses intense symbolic language and some images of judgment can admit more than one nuance of pastoral interpretation. The notes provided do not completely detail each zoological and military image, and do not allow to affirm with historical precision beyond what the text itself and the commentators cited say. It is also not possible to identify with certainty, only from the notes, how much of each element of the signal should be taken as literal or mainly figurative.
